claim: Intra-tissue genetic heterogeneity is universal to both healthy and cancerous tissues.
source: Intra-tissue genetic heterogeneity is universal to both healthy and cancerous tissues.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract without specific data provided in this manuscript.

claim: Intra-tissue genetic heterogeneity emerges from the stochastic accumulation of somatic mutations throughout development and homeostasis.
source: It emerges from the stochastic accumulation of somatic mutations throughout development and homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Bulk-derived variant allele frequency spectra (VAF) show transitions from growing to constant stem cell populations with age in samples of healthy esophagus epithelium.
source: Bulk-derived variant allele frequency spectra (VAF) show transitions from growing to constant stem cell populations with age in samples of healthy esophagus epithelium.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data analysis in Figure 2.

claim: Single-cell mutational burden distributions allow a sample size independent measure of mutation and proliferation rates.
source: Single-cell mutational burden distributions allow a sample size independent measure of mutation and proliferation rates.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through simulations in Figure 3.

claim: Mutation rates in adult hematopoietic stem cells are higher compared to inferences during development, suggesting additional proliferation-independent effects.
source: Mutation rates in adult hematopietic stem cells are higher compared to inferences during development, suggesting additional proliferation-independent effects.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by analysis in Figure 4a.

claim: In hematopoiesis, there are approximately 2 × 10^5 HSCs if all stem cells divide symmetrically.
source: In hematopiesis, we find approximately 2 × 105 HSCs, if all stem cells divide symmetrically.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by analysis in Figure 4c-d.

claim: The single-cell mutational burden distribution is over-dispersed compared to a model of Poisson distributed random mutations.
source: However, the single-cell mutational burden distribution is over-dispersed compared to a model of Poisson distributed random mutations.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: A time-associated model of mutation accumulation with a constant rate alone cannot generate the observed over-dispersed pattern of single-cell mutational burden.
source: A time-associated model of mutation accumulation with a constant rate alone cannot generate such a pattern.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed over-dispersion in the data.

claim: At least one additional source of stochasticity beyond constant mutation rates would be needed to explain the observed mutational burden distribution.
source: At least one additional source of stochasticity would be needed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inability of simple models to explain the data.

claim: Possible candidates for additional stochastic processes include occasional bursts of stem cell divisions, potentially in response to injury, or non-constant mutation rates.
source: Possible candidates for these processes may be occasional bursts of stem cell divisions, potentially in response to injury, or non-constant mutation rates either through environmental exposures or cell-intrinsic variation.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for the observed patterns.

claim: Intra-tissue genetic heterogeneity emerges from cells randomly accumulating mutations, self-renewing, differentiating, or dying, and clones of varying fitness competing and expanding.
source: Intra-tissue genetic heterogeneity emerges from a multitude of dynamical processes (Turajlic et al., 2019; Black and McGranahan, 2021). Cells randomly accumulate mutations, they self-renew, differentiate, or die and clones of varying fitness may compete and expand (Watson et al., 2020; Rulands et al., 2018; Werner et al., 2020; Gunnarsson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During early development, healthy somatic cells accumulate on average between 1.2 and 1.3 mutations per genome per division.
source: We know for example that during early development healthy somatic cells accumulate on average between 1.2 and 1.3 mutations per genome per division (Werner et al., 2020; Lee-Six et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The convergence towards equilibrium in VAF spectra slows down over time.
source: Interestingly, the convergence towards equilibrium slows down over time – for evenly-spaced observation times the solutions lie increasingly closer together – further decreasing the speed at which the high frequency portion of the spectrum approaches equilibrium.
evidence: This is observed in the numerical solutions presented in Figure 2a.

claim: There is a clear separation between the spectra of the youngest and middle age groups, but those of the middle and older groups are much closer.
source: Interestingly, while there is a clear separation between the spectra of the youngest and middle age groups, those of the middle and older groups are much closer.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 2b and agrees with theoretical predictions.

claim: Mutation rate estimates from esophagus data are in the range of 1–2 mutations per genome per cell division.
source: The estimates are in the range of 1–2 mutations per genome per cell division and agree with the previous observations based on early developmental stem cell divisions (Lee-Six et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figure 2c and compared to previous studies.

claim: There is a clear trend of a linearly increasing effective mutation rate with age in esophagus samples.
source: Surprisingly, we observe a clear trend of a linearly increasing effective mutation rate with age.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The mutational burden across individuals and tissues increases linearly with age.
source: It is well established that the mutational burden across individuals and tissues increases linearly with age (Cagan et al., 2022; Mitchell et al., 2022; Williams et al., 2022)
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: A continued slow linear increase of the stem cell population with age could explain the apparent increase in effective mutation rate.
source: An alternative explanation is a continued slow linear increase of the stem cell population with age (Figure 2d). In such a scenario, the effective mutation rate would appear to increase linearly with age as well, although the true mutation rate per cell division remains unchanged.
evidence: This is proposed as an alternative explanation and supported by simulations in Figure 2d.

claim: Direct in vivo imaging in multiple human tissues including esophagus support an increased density and slower proliferation of stem cells with age.
source: Direct in vivo imaging in multiple human tissues including esaphagus seem to support an increased density and slower proliferation of stem cells with age (Tomasetti et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: In a 59-year-old donor, hematopoietic stem cells had accumulated on average around 1000 mutations per cell.
source: Recent work by Lee-Six and colleagues (Lee-Six et al., 2018) showed that in a 59-year-old donor hematopoietic stem cells had accumulated on average around 1000 mutations per cell
evidence: This is cited from previous work by Lee-Six et al., 2018.

claim: There is significant variation in mutational burden between individual hematopoietic stem cell genomes, with some carrying 900 mutations and others up to 1200.
source: however, there was significant variation between individual genomes, some carrying 900 mutations, while others up to 1200.
evidence: This is cited from previous work by Lee-Six et al., 2018.

claim: Approximately 100 cells are sufficient to reliably reconstruct the mutational burden distribution.
source: Approximately, 100 cells are sufficient to reliably reconstruct the mutational burden distribution, which for example would constitute a small sample of the hematopoietic stem cell pool.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: The inference of mutational burden distribution does not significantly improve if data resolution is increased beyond a few hundred single cells.
source: In fact, the inference does not significantly improve if we increase data resolution beyond a few hundred single cells (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: The total division rate in the constant population phase of hematopoietic stem cells is λ=10.6 (7.6-15.3) divisions per HSC per year.
source: Using Equation 4 to estimate the expected number of divisions per lineage from the sample burden (SI 1.8.1), we find a total division rate (including both symmetric and asymmetric divisions) in the constant population phase of λ=10.6 (7.6-15.3) divisions per HSC per year, which is within ranges previously suggested (Watson et al., 2020; Dingli and Pacheco, 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from single-cell data from Lee-Six et al., 2018 using the methods developed in this study.

claim: The estimated mutation rate of 4.3 per cell per division is significantly higher compared to the 1.2 mutations per division suggested previously.
source: This is significantly higher compared to the 1.2 mutations per division suggested previously (Werner et al., 2020; Lee-Six et al., 2018).
evidence: This compares the current finding to previous estimates from cited literature.

claim: Many mutations in somatic tissue are acquired independently of cell divisions.
source: Recently, Mitchell and colleagues (Abascal et al., 2021) suggested that many mutations in somatic tissue are acquired independently of cell divisions.
evidence: This is cited from recent literature.

claim: The previous estimates of 1.2–1.3 mutations per genome per division were derived from early developmental cell divisions where the effects of aging would be negligible.
source: In fact, the previous estimates of 1.2–1.3 mutations per genome per division were derived from early developmental cell divisions where the effects of aging would be negligible.
evidence: This is an inference about the context of previous estimates.

claim: The increased mutation rate inferred in adult hematopoietic stem cells could in part be explained by proliferation-independent effects.
source: The increased mutation rate inferred here could in part be explained by proliferation-independent effects.
evidence: This is speculation based on recent literature about proliferation-independent mutations.

claim: The observed burden distribution is incompatible with a simple division-independent mutation model, which would lead to a Poisson distribution with much smaller variance.
source: Furthermore, the observed burden distribution is incompatible with a simple division-independent mutation model, which would lead to a Poisson distribution of the burdens that has a variance much smaller than what we observed (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the observed data in Figure 4a to theoretical expectations.

claim: The data is congruent with an adult HSC pool of at most 200,000–300,000 cells, depending on the exact timings of the maturation phase.
source: We find the data to be congruent with an adult HSC pool of at most 200'000–300'000 cells, depending on the exact timings of the maturation phase (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is inferred from fitting the model to data shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: The upper bound of HSC pool size corresponds to the case of exclusively symmetric stem cell divisions.
source: However, this upper bound corresponds to the case of exclusively symmetric stem cell divisions.
evidence: This is an inference from the model fitting shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The data would be consistent with 50,000 stem cells if 90% (p=0.9) of all stem cell divisions are asymmetric.
source: For example, the data would be consistent with 50'000 stem cells if 90% (p=0.9) of all stem cell divisions are asymmetric.
evidence: This is inferred from the model fitting shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Non-developmental branchings are observed in the data, which implies that not all HSC divisions can be asymmetric (p<1).
source: We note that in the data non-developmental branchings are observed, which immediately implies that not all HSC divisions can be asymmetric (p<1) and thus a scenario of an extremely small population of only a handful of HSCs maintaining hematopoisis can be rejected.
evidence: This is an inference from observed features in the data.

claim: Watson and colleagues estimated 25,000 as a reasonable lower bound for the number of HSCs using a population-based method.
source: With an orthogonal population-based method, Watson and colleagues estimated 25'000 as a reasonable lower bound for the number of HSCs.
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: If the HSC pool size is 25,000, this would imply 0.95 as an upper bound for the proportion of all stem cell divisions that are asymmetric.
source: Based on our inference, this would imply 0.95 as an upper bound for the proportion of all stem cell divisions that are asymmetric.
evidence: This is an inference combining the current model with previous estimates.

claim: Single-cell and bulk whole genome sequencing inform on different aspects of somatic evolution.
source: Here, we have shown that single-cell and bulk whole genome sequencing can inform on different aspects of somatic evolution.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the results presented.

claim: Single-cell information supports previous bulk-based estimates of possible ranges of HSC numbers.
source: Single-cell information does support previous bulk-based estimates of possible ranges of HSC numbers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current results to previous estimates.

claim: The mutation rate inference during homeostasis from single-cell data is approximately four times higher compared to previous developmental estimates.
source: Surprisingly, the same single-cell data leads to a mutation rate inference during homeostasis is approximately four times higher compared to previous developmental estimates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis presented in Figure 4a.

claim: Evidence is emerging that positively selected variants in blood are almost universally present in individuals above 60.
source: Evidence is emerging that positively selected variants in blood are almost universally present in individuals above 60, while the effective observable dynamics in younger individuals is well described by neutral dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as emerging evidence from the field.

claim: A time-dependent model of mutation accumulation with constant rate across all cells predicts Poisson distributed single-cell mutational burdens.
source: We note that for a time-dependent rate of mutation accumulation that is constant across all cells at a given point in time, this model predicts Poisson distributed single-cell mutational burdens.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model.

claim: The single-cell mutational burden distribution in human HSCs is highly over-dispersed compared to a Poisson model.
source: In contrast, we find the single-cell mutational burden distribution in human HSCs to be highly over-dispersed compared to a Poisson model.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Current theoretical models of somatic evolution in healthy tissues are incomplete.
source: Either way, our observations suggest that our current theoretical models of somatic evolution in healthy tissues are incomplete.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inability of current models to explain the observed over-dispersion.

claim: There is evidence for unknown processes contributing to intra-tissue genetic heterogeneity.
source: There is evidence for unknown processes contributing to intra-tissue genetic heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the discrepancies between model predictions and observations.

claim: The constant-size equilibrium establishes earliest at the lowest frequencies and moves to higher frequency over time.
source: Over time the shape changes as a wavelike front traveling from low to high frequency, with the constant-size equilibrium establishing earliest at the lowest frequencies and moving to higher frequency overtime.
evidence: This is observed in the numerical solutions shown in Figure 2a.

claim: More complex forms of demographic changes result in qualitatively similar VAF behavior to the simple growth-to-constant model.
source: More complex forms of such demographic changes, for example, the inclusion of a mixed growth-and-maintenance phase or a logistically growing population, result in qualitatively similar behavior (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through additional simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The estimators for mutation and proliferation rates only require information on comparably few single cells.
source: More importantly, they only require information on comparably few single cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations in Figure 3a and b.

claim: Strong sampling changes the shape of the expected VAF distribution.
source: In contrast with the mutational burden distribution, strong sampling changes the shape of the expected distribution.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c comparing population and sampled VAF spectra.

claim: The variance in the VAF distribution increases with variant frequency f.
source: Furthermore, from stochastic simulations we note that the variance in the distribution increases with variant frequency f, making the lowest frequency state (i.e. 1/S) the best candidate for comparative fitting and evolutionary inferences (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The data is consistent with 50,000 stem cells if 90% of all stem cell divisions are asymmetric.
source: Accounting for the possibility of mutating asymmetric divisions reduces the estimated stem cell pool. For example, the data would be consistent with 50'000 stem cells if 90% (p=0.9) of all stem cell divisions are asymmetric.
evidence: This is inferred from the model fitting shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Even smaller stem cell pool sizes are possible, though decreasing an order of magnitude would imply an extremely large portion (>99%) of asymmetric HSC divisions.
source: In principle, even smaller stem cell pool sizes are possible, though decreasing an order of magnitude would imply an extremely large portion (gt99%) of asymmetric HSC divisions.
evidence: This is an inference from the model fitting shown in Figure 4c.

claim: A scenario of an extremely small population of only a handful of HSCs maintaining hematopoiesis can be rejected.
source: We note that in the data non-developmental branchings are observed, which immediately implies that not all HSC divisions can be asymmetric (p<1) and thus a scenario of an extremely small population of only a handful of HSCs maintaining hematopoisis can be rejected.
evidence: This is an inference from observed features in the data.

claim: A combination of division-independent mutations together with non-Poissonian cell divisions could possibly reproduce the observed mutational burden distribution.
source: A combination of division-independent mutations together with non-Poissonian cell divisions could possibly reproduce the result.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for the observed patterns.

claim: A linear increase in stem cell population would emerge from a small bias of stem cells towards self-renewal and a slowdown of proliferation rate proportional to the change in population size.
source: However, such a linear increase would emerge from a small bias of stem cells towards self-renewal (growth) and concomitantly a slowdown of the stem cell proliferation rate proportional to the change in population size (Werner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous theoretical work.

claim: A feedback of decreased cell proliferation with increasing population size would function as a tumor suppressor mechanism.
source: This explanation is attractive for another reason: A feedback of decreased cell proliferation with increasing population size would also function as a tumor suppressor mechanism, and maybe another reason cancer driver mutations in healthy tissues are abundant but rarely progress to cancer (Martincorena et al., 2018; Martincorena et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about the biological implications of the proposed mechanism, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Cancer progression would require additional genomic or environmental changes to overcome regulatory feedback.
source: Progression would require additional genomic or environmental changes to overcome this regulatory feedback.
evidence: This is speculation about cancer progression mechanisms.

claim: The single-cell mutational burden alone cannot disentangle symmetric and asymmetric division rates.
source: Notably, the single-cell mutational burden alone cannot disentangle symmetric and asymmetric division rates.
evidence: This is a limitation of the method identified through theoretical analysis.

claim: Most recent estimates suggest a hematopoietic stem cell population size of 10^5 cells.
source: For example, although the exact number of HSCs remains unknown, most recent estimates suggest a population size of 105 cells (Watson et al., 2020; Lee-Six et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: In tumors, the number of cells can be as large as 10^10 cells.
source: In tumors, this number can be as large as 1010 cells (Werner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: If a small sample is used to construct the VAF spectrum, the distribution of variants will be significantly transformed with respect to that of the total population.
source: If we, however, construct the VAF spectrum from such a small sample, the distribution of variants will be significantly transformed with respect to that of the total population (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3c.

claim: The lowest frequency state (1/S) is the best candidate for comparative fitting due to lower variance.
source: Furthermore, from stochastic simulations we note that the variance in the distribution increases with variant frequency f, making the lowest frequency state (i.e. 1/S) the best candidate for comparative fitting and evolutionary inferences (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations arising during early phases are more likely to be found at higher frequencies upon measurement.
source: This is partly because mutations arising during these phases are more likely to be found at higher frequencies upon measurement (Poon et al., 2021; Werner, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The estimate of HSC pool size agrees with the original study and other independent inferences based on population data.
source: This estimate agrees with the original study and other independent inferences based on population data (Watson et al., 2020; Lee-Six et al., 2018).
evidence: This compares the current findings to previous estimates from cited literature.

claim: The earliest hematopoietic cells appear 16 days post-conception.
source: Note that this size is expected to be relatively small, as the earliest hematopoietic cells appear 16 days post-conception (Ivanovs et al., 2017)
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Peripheral blood is already driven mostly by functional HSCs by 14 weeks post conception.
source: and peripheral blood is already driven mostly by functional HSC's by 14 weeks post conception (Spencer Chapman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Growth and Moran divisions on average add twice as many mutations to a lineage as asymmetric divisions.
source: Thus, we find that the growth and Moran divisions on average add twice as many mutations to a lineage as the asymmetric divisions.
evidence: This is derived mathematically in the methods section.
